title: My experience. Build metal not art.
author: Qkrooz
selftext:
AI is here, and it won't leave.  
Basically, it gave us superpowers. We can ship a game in months. We made the market even more competitive, so we need to focus on what AI cannot do: **ART, NARRATIVES**.

Dev here. I have been creating my game since 2020—around 4 years of day-and-night development without rest, and without any AI.  
Then one day, agentic AI appeared, and I noticed a ton of things I was doing wrong. So I put all my hard-earned knowledge into an Obsidian vault and then fed it to the AI. It took around one month. And then I could basically ship a game from my head to the Google Play Store in **ONE DAY**.

So that was the true advantage: metal.

I noticed that AI **CAN'T DO ART**, and if it can, it's obvious—then players hate it.

In my experience, we have a big opportunity in our hands. We have the blessing to focus on narrative, art, and animations in order to bring great products to life.

Finally, I believe we need to avoid putting "made with AI" in the titles. Just focus on gameplay.

Remember, we're doing **G-A-M-E-S**—they need to be fun, not complex. They have to provide experiences: psychological experiences, horror experiences, funny experiences. Do not try to build the next *Zelda*, the next *Mario*, or the next *Doom*—break the mold. Go for it.

comments.author: Dumpfumpkin
comments.body: I use AI to create visual assets. I’m not trying to make art. My goal is to make videos games that are fun to play with my friends and family. I don’t need my game to be commercially successful because this is a hobby to me. If I can play my game with my buds and we have a good time, it was a success. If I can sell a few copies to others who also might think it’s fun, even better.

replies.author: BrokenLoadOrder
replies.body: Which is awesome for you, but my impression is that 90% of this sub is about commercial development. In that case, yes, using AI for visual assets is shooting yourself in the foot. Players avoid that like the plague, with a large study of Steam releases suggesting a 50% decline in sales from those that use AI art assets compared to not.

replies.author: BrokenLoadOrder
replies.body:
Considering AI art is pretty obvious, I'm not sure disclosure matters in that instance.

Sins of a Solar Empire 2 hasn't disclosed AI usage, but everyone is well aware that the placeholder art is AI generated.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
So, I agree in a lot ways. I do think AI can produce visual assets. But I get its help with things like shaders (math, computations, etc) , procedural terrain and how one terrain should react near other terrain, etc.  It CAN do very simple modeling, coloring, whatever... But I don't know why anyone would waste tokens on it when it takes so much longer than doing it by hand, and there's a reasonable chance you'll have to fix things up to maintain quality anyway.

What it does do very well though, and my primary use in my art pipeline, is  creating tools for me to use. For instance, I model my characters.. but Blender, while great, adds a lot of extra steps to get a character from there to game. Sooo, I had AI help build a sculpting rig to ease morph creations for my humanoid characters that all run on the same skeleton. Instant feedback, can see them react to the game's lighting and shaders, immediately add or remove the sculpts as morph targets, test against the existing animation suite, etc.

Huge time saver.  I even had it create me a terrain tool for my game which leverages my favorite material maker / substance painter nodes, the ones I found myself constantly using for my style, and now have it in game where I can see the material in the exact lighting scenarios, with easy access to existing palette choices.. I can prototype a material and immediately apply it to a prefabbed structure, replacing other materials present and see how it looks.

I'll probably eventually bundle these things in as modding tools for the game as well. Absolutely massive time saver.

That being said, not very useful unless someone is willing to get down and dirty and actually do the manual work. Still requires artistic sense. Eventually I think AI will be able to use these same tools to produce better results than sculpting or painting by hand, but I don't feel it's there yet. I've had it use the terrain tool to throw out 10-20 material styles, and it did a reasonable job picking some colors, brushstroke masks, behaviour dial values, etc. But I still had to edit them all. It will make silly decisions like decide that sand or gravel should behave like stone, even though one is solid and the other is particulate.  I did find it did a much better job when I gave it references to work with AND the tool.  But a lot of time there really is no reference that is adequate with a stylized game so.. eh. I'm content to do the manual work on it. There are few things more satisfying then seeing a piece realized in game. I'm happy to let the AI squash bugs and build tools that I would beat my head against a wall for days to resolve myself.
